A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLoVE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification, reconstruction, mixed linear regression, initialization, scalability, and ablation experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds FEMNIST, unknown-cluster-count, early-stopping, partial-participation, scalability, and FINCH comparisons.

M1.justification: V1 requires a known cluster count and continues clustering throughout training. V2 Algorithms 1–2 introduce cluster-count selection using silhouette scores, stopping clustering after assignment stability, and assigning subsequent clients using saved models and centroids. These substantially extend the procedure; random client subsampling itself already existed in v1.

E1.justification: V2 adds FEMNIST classification with individual writers as clients and evaluates intermittent participation, including rounds with fewer participating clients than true clusters. These extend the represented client population and operating conditions. The original image, text, reconstruction, and synthetic regression coverage remains.

E2.justification: The main comparator set remains, with CFL renamed CFL-S. V2 adds FINCH versus k-means as a clustering-component comparison. IFCA curves disappear from the corresponding MNIST convergence plot, v1 Figure 5(a) versus v2 Figure 7, although IFCA remains in scalability tables. FedGWC is discussed but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The reported general batch size changes from 100 to 64. Convergence tables replace percentage of final ARI attained with absolute ARI at round 10. Added protocols include unknown-K initialization, stopping after three unchanged rounds, participation-dependent ARI evaluation, and scaling to 1000 clients versus 200 in v1's scaling plot. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds analyses of unknown cluster counts, early stopping, partial participation, and FINCH versus k-means, and substantially expands scalability testing. These examine practical assumptions and component sensitivity beyond v1. The original initialization, matching, agglomerative-clustering, square-root-loss, and averaging analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions generally specify three seeds and mean plus standard deviation. However, v2 Appendix E.5 describes Table 18 as reporting mean and variance, without reconciling this with the general policy. It is unclear whether this introduces a different uncertainty statistic or is a wording error; no increased run count is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results, including FEMNIST accuracy of 68.2 ± 1.3 and new cluster-count, stopping, participation, scaling, and FINCH results. Convergence entries also change: IFCA's reported first ARI ≥0.9 round for MNIST label skew 1 changes from 2.0 ± 0.0 to never reached. Most original accuracy and reconstruction-loss entries remain unchanged; changed metrics and settings preclude interpreting the revisions as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Theorems 4.1–4.2 and Appendix A's mathematical definitions, bounds, lemmas, and proofs are retained. The expanded assumptions and random, nearly orthogonal initialization explanation bring existing appendix material into the main exposition. No new theoretical guarantee is supplied for the added practical variants.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about loss embeddings, initialization robustness, supervised/unsupervised applicability, and linear-setting convergence remain. The introduction and conclusion extend the claimed practical advantages to sparse participation, stragglers, and low communication and computation overhead.

C2.justification: V1's categorical assertion that loss vectors reveal no client data becomes a qualified discussion of underexplored leakage and possible differential-privacy tradeoffs in v2 Appendix C. V2 also adds overhead and memory arguments, explains FedAvg's advantage under overlapping label distributions, and softens the unsupervised superiority statement to match the retained losses. The earlier explanation attributing client-count scaling benefits to longer loss vectors is removed.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-access URL for CLoVE and the self-implemented baselines, previously listed only as self-implemented. It adds an experiment-specific client/sample-count table, details Dirichlet allocation for the main label-skew experiments, and states default initialization. Hardware and Python/PyTorch versions remain unchanged. These are substantial documentation improvements, without establishing changes to every underlying experiment.

R1.justification: V2 adds FedGWC positioning in related work and Appendix C.3, plus FINCH, FEMNIST/LEAF, and matching references, while removing the UNEXT motivation. It also introduces explicit priority claims concerning extensive unsupervised evaluation and autoencoder clustering. Most of the existing literature discussion remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, main section sequence, and much existing prose remain. Revisions concentrate on the comparative introduction, method exposition, assumptions, and experimental setup. The main-text ablation summary is removed while its appendix content remains, and appendices are reorganized around the added algorithm and discussion sections.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main paper, redraws Figure 1 with an additional loss-vector illustration, and merges v1's image and text accuracy tables into Table 1. It adds protocol/result tables and participation plots, expands algorithm displays, and separates and redraws the original combined convergence figure. These substantially alter the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important practical gaps in v1 through explicit procedures and experiments for unknown cluster counts, sparse participation, early stopping, and larger client populations. Code-access information and detailed experimental specifications improve reproducibility, while the revised privacy discussion corrects an overly categorical assurance. Cost savings still lack direct measurements, and batch-size and uncertainty-reporting ambiguities remain, but the gains in practical validation and transparency are substantial.
